Esmolol is a Group 2 antiarrhythmic. It functions as a short-acting, cardioselective beta-1 adrenoceptor antagonist, primarily reducing heart rate and AV nodal conduction through inhibition of sympathetic effects rather than direct sodium channel blockade.

Flecainide is the prototype Group 1C antiarrhythmic. While it blocks sodium channels, it is distinguished from 1B agents by having no significant effect on action potential duration and a very slow dissociation rate from the channel.

Mexiletine is a Group 1B drug, an orally active analog of lidocaine. It selectively binds to sodium channels in the inactivated state, which is prevalent in ischemic or depolarized tissue, and typically shortens the action potential duration.
citation: In book "Mini Katzung", Page 125 (Book Page): [Mexiletine is an orally active 1B agent. These drugs selectively affect ischemic or depolarized Purkinje and ventricular tissue and have little effect on atrial tissue; the drugs reduce AP duration in some cells...]

category: Classify anti arrhythmic drugs
statement: A patient is prescribed an antiarrhythmic that functions by inhibiting the outward repolarizing potassium current (IKr) during Phase 3 of the cardiac action potential. What is the fundamental electrophysiological consequence of this Group 3 classification?
options: Shortening of the QT interval on the surface electrocardiogram
Marked slowing of the Phase 0 upstroke velocity in ventricular cells
Decrease in the slope of Phase 4 depolarization in SA node cells
Inhibition of L-type calcium channels leading to slowed AV conduction
Prolongation of the effective refractory period through increased action potential duration
correctOption: Prolongation of the effective refractory period through increased action potential duration
optionExplanations: Group 3 agents invariably prolong the QT interval because the QT interval is the surface ECG representation of ventricular action potential duration; shortening the QT interval would be more characteristic of Group 1B drugs in certain tissues.

Slowing the Phase 0 upstroke velocity is the defining feature of Group 1 drugs (Sodium channel blockers). Group 3 drugs typically have minimal effects on the upstroke velocity unless they have mixed properties like Amiodarone.

Decreasing the slope of Phase 4 depolarization is a characteristic of Group 2 (Beta-blockers) and Group 4 (Calcium channel blockers) agents, which suppress abnormal automaticity rather than Phase 3 repolarization.

Inhibition of L-type calcium channels is the mechanism for Group 4 agents (e.g., Verapamil). While Amiodarone (Class 3) has some calcium-blocking activity, it is not the primary definition of the Group 3 classification.

By blocking potassium channels responsible for repolarization, Group 3 drugs extend the time the cell remains in a depolarized state. This lengthens the action potential duration and, consequently, the effective refractory period, preventing premature re-excitation.
citation: In book "Mini Katzung", Page 127 (Book Page): [The hallmark of group 3 drugs is prolongation of the AP duration. This AP prolongation is caused by blockade of the IK potassium channels, chiefly IKr, that are responsible for the repolarization of the AP... AP prolongation results in an increase in effective refractory period...]

category: Classify anti arrhythmic drugs
statement: When contrasting the sub-classifications of Group 1 antiarrhythmic drugs, which physiological parameter distinguishes Group 1A agents from Group 1C agents?
options: Effect on the action potential duration (APD)
Ability to suppress abnormal ventricular pacemakers
Sensitivity to the extracellular potassium concentration
Effect on the Phase 0 sodium current magnitude
Presence of local anesthetic activity
correctOption: Effect on the action potential duration (APD)
optionExplanations: The primary differentiator is APD: Group 1A drugs prolong APD by blocking potassium channels ($I_K$), whereas Group 1C drugs have no significant effect on APD or the QT interval.
Both 1A and 1C drugs are capable of suppressing ectopic pacemakers by shifting the threshold for excitation or slowing phase 4 depolarization in non-nodal tissues.
Both groups are sensitive to potassium levels; hyperkalemia generally increases the toxicity and sodium channel-blocking efficacy of all Group 1 drugs.
Both Group 1A and Group 1C significantly reduce the magnitude of the Phase 0 sodium current ($I_{Na}$); however, Group 1C drugs are typically more potent depressants of this current.
Local anesthetic activity (membrane stabilization) is a general property shared by all Group 1 drugs, as they all function by binding to and inhibiting voltage-gated sodium channels ($I_{Na}$).
citation: In book "Mini Katzung", Page 124 (Book Page): [Group 1A agents (prototype procainamide) prolong the AP. Group 1B drugs (prototype lidocaine) shorten the AP in some cardiac tissues... Group 1C drugs (prototype flecainide) have no effect on AP duration.]

category: Classify anti arrhythmic drugs
statement: A 64-year-old male with a history of recurrent ventricular tachycardia is treated with a medication that has the longest half-life among antiarrhythmics. He recently developed yellowish-brown microcrystalline deposits in his cornea and symptoms of hyperthyroidism. According to the classification of this drug, what is its primary group and its unique pharmacodynamic profile?
options: Group 3; Combined blockade of K+, Na+, Ca2+ channels and Beta receptors
Group 2; Selective Beta-1 receptor antagonism with short-term efficacy
Group 4; Selective L-type calcium channel blockade in the AV node
Group 1A; Pure sodium channel blockade with antimuscarinic effects
Group 1C; Powerful sodium current depression without APD changes
correctOption: Group 3; Combined blockade of K+, Na+, Ca2+ channels and Beta receptors
optionExplanations: The drug is Amiodarone. Although primarily classified as Group 3 due to its potassium channel blockade and APD prolongation, its unique clinical profile stems from its broad-spectrum 'multi-group' actions (1, 2, 3, and 4).

The clinical presentation (corneal deposits, thyroid issues, long half-life) is inconsistent with Group 2 drugs like Propranolol or Esmolol, which have much shorter half-lives and lack these systemic toxicities.
Group 4 drugs like Verapamil cause constipation and peripheral edema but do not cause corneal deposits or thyroid dysfunction. Their half-life is measured in hours, not weeks.

While Amiodarone has 1A-like effects on sodium channels, it is not a pure 1A drug. 1A drugs like Disopyramide cause antimuscarinic effects, but Amiodarone does not; it also lacks the iodine-related thyroid toxicity seen here.
Group 1C drugs like Flecainide increase the QRS duration but do not typically cause the extra-cardiac toxicities described in the scenario, and they do not prolong the action potential duration.
citation: In book "Mini Katzung", Page 127 (Book Page): [Amiodarone... is usually classified as a group 3 drug... It blocks sodium, calcium, and potassium channels and β adrenoceptors... Amiodarone causes microcrystalline deposits in the cornea... thyroid dysfunction... longest half-life of all antiarrhythmic drugs (weeks).]

category: Classify anti arrhythmic drugs
statement: An intravenous bolus of a miscellaneous antiarrhythmic is administered to a patient to terminate an acute paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia. The drug works by increasing the diastolic potassium current (IK) in the atrioventricular (AV) node. What is the pharmacological classification and expected duration of effect of this agent?
options: Group 4; 6-8 hours
Miscellaneous; 10-15 seconds
Group 3; 7 hours
Group 2; 10 minutes
Group 1B; 1-2 hours
correctOption: Miscellaneous; 10-15 seconds
optionExplanations: Group 4 drugs (e.g., Verapamil) also act on the AV node but they inhibit calcium currents rather than activating potassium currents, and their duration is several hours, making them unsuitable for the '15-second' profile of Adenosine.

Adenosine is classified in the 'Miscellaneous' group. It acts on A1 receptors to increase outward potassium flow and decrease inward calcium flow, leading to transient hyperpolarization and AV block. Its ultra-short half-life results in a duration of ~15 seconds.

Group 3 drugs (e.g., Dofetilide) have durations of many hours and are used for rhythm control in atrial fibrillation, not for the acute, bolus-mediated termination of SVT via AV nodal hyperpolarization.
Esmolol is a Group 2 agent with a short duration (10 minutes), but it works via beta-receptor blockade and reducing cAMP, not through direct hyperpolarization via I-K activation.
Group 1B drugs (e.g., Lidocaine) have no effect on the AV node or supraventricular arrhythmias; they act on sodium channels in the ventricles and have a duration of 1-2 hours.
citation: In book "Mini Katzung", Page 128 (Book Page): [Adenosine... when given in high doses (6–12 mg) as an intravenous bolus, the drug markedly slows or completely blocks conduction in the atrioventricular node... by hyperpolarizing this tissue (through increased IK)... has an extremely short duration of action (about 15 seconds).]

category: Classify anti arrhythmic drugs
statement: Which of the following drug pairs represents the standard Group 4 classification of antiarrhythmics, acting specifically on calcium-dependent cardiac tissues?
options: Procainamide and Quinidine
Verapamil and Diltiazem
Nifedipine and Amlodipine
Sotalol and Ibutilide
Lidocaine and Mexiletine
correctOption: Verapamil and Diltiazem
optionExplanations: Procainamide and Quinidine are Group 1A antiarrhythmics. They primarily block sodium channels and some potassium channels, but do not act as primary calcium channel blockers in the Singh-Vaughan Williams classification.
Verapamil and Diltiazem are non-dihydropyridines. They have a high affinity for calcium channels in the SA and AV nodes, making them effective antiarrhythmics for supraventricular tachycardias.

Nifedipine and Amlodipine are dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers. They are not used as antiarrhythmics because they primarily cause vasodilation, which triggers reflex sympathetic discharge that can exacerbate arrhythmias.
Sotalol and Ibutilide are Group 3 antiarrhythmics. Their primary mechanism is the blockade of potassium channels ($I_K$), leading to prolongation of the action potential duration.
Lidocaine and Mexiletine are Group 1B sodium channel blockers. They are used for ventricular arrhythmias and do not significantly affect the calcium-dependent nodes.
citation: In book "Mini Katzung", Page 128 (Book Page): [Group 4 Antiarrhythmics (Calcium L-type Channel Blockers)... Verapamil is the prototype. Diltiazem is also an effective antiarrhythmic drug. Nifedipine and the other dihydropyridines are not useful as antiarrhythmics...]

category: Classify anti arrhythmic drugs
statement: The concept of 'use-dependent' or 'state-dependent' blockade is fundamental to the classification of Group 1 antiarrhythmics. This phenomenon suggests that these drugs have the highest affinity for sodium channels in which of the following states?
options: Permanently closed
Inactivated or Open
Primed and ready for activation
Resting and fully repolarized
Hyperpolarized and non-conducting
correctOption: Inactivated or Open
optionExplanations: Sodium channels are dynamic proteins; there is no 'permanently closed' physiological state. Drugs only interact with the existing cycling states (Resting, Open, Inactivated).

Group 1 drugs preferentially bind to sodium channels that are either open (during Phase 0) or inactivated (during Phase 2). Tachycardias increase the frequency of these states, thereby increasing drug binding and effect.
The 'primed' state is essentially the resting state at the end of diastole. As stated, Group 1 drugs bind 'much less readily' when the channel is in this fully repolarized/resting state.

Binding to the resting state is minimal. If drugs bound primarily to resting channels, they would cause toxic blockade of normal heart tissue at all rates, lacking the selectivity needed for antiarrhythmic effects.
Hyperpolarization stabilizes the resting state. Sodium channel blockers dissociate from the channel during the resting/hyperpolarized phase; thus, hyperpolarized tissue is less affected.
citation: In book "Mini Katzung", Page 124 (Book Page): [Useful sodium channel-blocking drugs bind to their receptors readily when the channel is open or inactivated and much less readily when it is fully repolarized and resting... They are use dependent or state dependent in their action...]

category: Classify anti arrhythmic drugs
statement: A 52-year-old female is being treated for a persistent arrhythmia. Her ECG shows a significant increase in the PR interval, a markedly widened QRS complex, and a prolonged QT interval. Following a suicidal ingestion of her medication, she develops severe hypotension and a wide-complex rhythm. According to the Singh-Vaughan Williams classification, which drug was she most likely taking, and what is the treatment of choice for her overdose?
options: Procainamide; Concentrated Sodium Lactate
Lidocaine; Intravenous Sodium Bicarbonate
Flecainide; Digoxin Antibodies
Verapamil; Calcium Gluconate
Atenolol; Glucagon
correctOption: Procainamide; Concentrated Sodium Lactate
optionExplanations: Procainamide is a Group 1A drug that increases PR, QRS, and QT intervals. Toxicity involves severe conduction slowing (wide QRS). Sodium lactate helps by increasing the sodium gradient and potentially displacing the drug from receptors through alkalinization.

Lidocaine (1B) typically does not widen the QRS or prolong the QT interval in normal tissue. Sodium bicarbonate is used for TCA toxicity, but lactate is the specific recommendation for Group 1A overdose here.
Flecainide (Group 1C) markedly widens the QRS but does not prolong the QT interval (APD). Digoxin antibodies are for digitalis glycoside toxicity, not sodium channel blocker overdose.
Verapamil (Group 4) would increase the PR interval but would not widen the QRS complex or prolong the QT interval (ventricular depolarization/repolarization).

Atenolol (Group 2) increases the PR interval and slows the heart rate but does not cause QRS widening or QT prolongation. Glucagon is the antidote for beta-blocker overdose, but the ECG findings don't match.
citation: In book "Mini Katzung", Page 126 (Book Page): [Procainamide... At high doses they may slow AV conduction (increased PR)... increase the QRS duration... prolong the AP duration (increased QT)... Treatment of overdose... concentrated sodium lactate (to reverse drug-induced arrhythmias)...]

category: Classify anti arrhythmic drugs
statement: Sotalol is an antiarrhythmic agent that exhibits a dual-mechanism classification. Based on the Singh-Vaughan Williams system, which two classes describe its pharmacological profile?
options: Group 1C and Group 3
Group 2 and Group 3
Group 3 and Miscellaneous
Group 1A and Group 2
Group 3 and Group 4
correctOption: Group 2 and Group 3
optionExplanations: Sotalol prolongs the action potential, which is the opposite of a Group 1C effect (1C has no effect on APD) and Sotalol lacks the strong sodium channel blockade of 1C.
Sotalol is unique because it combines non-selective beta-adrenoceptor blockade (Group 2) with potassium channel blockade ($I_{Kr}$) that prolongs the action potential (Group 3).
Sotalol is a standard Singh-Vaughan Williams drug with well-defined targets (Beta receptors and K-channels); it is not relegated to the Miscellaneous group like Adenosine or Magnesium.
While Sotalol prolongs the action potential like Group 1A drugs, it does not have the sodium-channel blocking property that defines Group 1A.
Sotalol has no significant L-type calcium channel blocking activity; therefore, it does not belong to Group 4.
citation: In book "Mini Katzung", Page 127 (Book Page): [Sotalol is a chiral compound... One isomer is an effective β blocker (Group 2), and both isomers contribute to the antiarrhythmic action through K-channel block (Group 3).]

category: Classify anti arrhythmic drugs
statement: Which of the following drugs is classified as a prototype Group 2 antiarrhythmic, primarily indicated for prophylaxis against sudden death ventricular fibrillation post-myocardial infarction?
options: Verapamil
Amiodarone
Propranolol
Procainamide
Adenosine
correctOption: Propranolol
optionExplanations: Verapamil is a Group 4 drug (Calcium channel blocker). It is used for supraventricular arrhythmias and is not the drug of choice for preventing ventricular fibrillation post-MI.
Amiodarone is primarily Group 3. While it has some beta-blocking properties, Propranolol is the historical prototype of Group 2 specified for post-MI prophylaxis in this text.
Propranolol is the prototypic Group 2 (Beta-blocker). It reduces sympathetic stimulation of the heart, which is critical in preventing triggered arrhythmias in the post-infarction setting.
Procainamide is a Group 1A drug. While used for arrhythmias after MI, it is not a Group 2 agent and carries a higher risk of proarrhythmia.
Adenosine is a miscellaneous agent used for the acute termination of supraventricular tachycardia; it has no role in the chronic prophylaxis of ventricular fibrillation.
citation: In book "Mini Katzung", Page 132 (Book Page): [Group 2... Propranolol... Postmyocardial infarction as prophylaxis against sudden death ventricular fibrillation...]

category: Define Coronary Steal Phenomenon
statement: Regarding the clinical pharmacology of antianginal agents, why is the term 'coronary vasodilator' currently considered an 'older, incorrect name' for drugs used in angina pectoris?
options: Because some potent coronary vasodilators are actually ineffective in relieving angina.
Because the primary mechanism is always the reduction of cardiac work, not vasodilation.
Because coronary vessels are already maximally dilated in a healthy heart.
Because these drugs only act on peripheral veins to reduce preload.
Because coronary vasodilation is always accompanied by dangerous hypertension.
correctOption: Because some potent coronary vasodilators are actually ineffective in relieving angina.
optionExplanations: Correct. The text explicitly identifies 'coronary vasodilator' as an older, incorrect term because certain potent vasodilators do not effectively treat angina and may even worsen it through mechanisms like coronary steal.

Incorrect. While reducing cardiac work is a primary strategy for effort angina, increasing oxygen delivery via vasodilation remains a valid secondary strategy in vasospastic angina, so the term isn't incorrect because of mechanism priority.

Incorrect. Coronary vessels have significant reserve and are not always maximally dilated; however, in ischemic zones, they may be dilated due to local metabolites, which contributes to the steal phenomenon when other vessels dilate.

Incorrect. While nitrates do act on peripheral veins to reduce preload, the term 'coronary vasodilator' is not incorrect solely because of this; it is incorrect because not all coronary vasodilators provide therapeutic relief.
Incorrect. Vasodilators generally cause a reduction in blood pressure (hypotension), not hypertension, although they may cause reflex tachycardia.
citation: In book "Mini Katzung", Page 104 (Book Page): Coronary vasodilator: Older, incorrect name for drugs useful in angina; some potent coronary vasodilators are ineffective in angina

category: Define Coronary Steal Phenomenon
statement: In the pathophysiology of myocardial ischemia, which mechanism explains how certain potent vasodilators may fail to improve perfusion to ischemic areas compared to nitrates?
options: Potent vasodilators may decrease flow through collateral vessels in ischemic areas.
Nitrates inhibit mitochondrial aldehyde dehydrogenase, preventing coronary steal.
Nitrates increase coronary flow specifically via collateral vessels in ischemic areas.
Potent vasodilators increase the double product by reducing systolic blood pressure.
Potent vasodilators only act on the venous system, bypassing the arterial supply.
correctOption: Nitrates increase coronary flow specifically via collateral vessels in ischemic areas.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. While the 'steal' phenomenon involves diverting blood away, the text focuses on why nitrates are *effective* (via collaterals), implying 'potent' dilators lack this specific redistributive benefit.
Incorrect. Nitrates *require* mitochondrial aldehyde dehydrogenase (ALDH2) to release nitric oxide; they do not inhibit it to prevent steal.

Correct. Nitrates are effective because they can increase flow through collateral vessels to the ischemic zones, a specific distributive benefit that 'potent' global vasodilators may lack, leading to the steal phenomenon.
Incorrect. Reducing systolic blood pressure typically *decreases* the double product (cardiac work), although reflex tachycardia might offset this.
Incorrect. Potent vasodilators like nifedipine act primarily on arterioles, not just the venous system, but this arteriolar focus is part of why they can cause 'steal'.
citation: In book "Mini Katzung", Page 107 (Book Page): A secondary mechanism—namely, an increase in coronary flow via collateral vessels in ischemic areas—may also contribute.

category: Define Coronary Steal Phenomenon
coreConcept: Reflex Sympathetic Response vs. Myocardial Perfusion
statement: Contrast the effects of nitrates and potent rapid-acting arteriolar vasodilators (like prompt-release nifedipine) on myocardial oxygen delivery and requirement. Which of the following is a primary reason for the 'ineffective' nature of global vasodilators in angina?
options: They may evoke reflex sympathetic discharge that increases oxygen requirement faster than delivery.
They stimulate alpha-receptors, causing paradoxical coronary vasospasm.
They reduce large artery stiffness, which paradoxically increases afterload.
They cause a decrease in heart rate, prolonging the ejection time.
They increase diastolic filling pressure, leading to higher fiber tension.
correctOption: They may evoke reflex sympathetic discharge that increases oxygen requirement faster than delivery.
optionExplanations: Correct. Potent vasodilators cause a sudden drop in BP, triggering a reflex sympathetic discharge that increases heart rate and contractility. This spike in oxygen demand can exceed any increase in oxygen delivery, leading to ischemia.
Incorrect. These drugs are calcium channel blockers or direct vasodilators; they do not stimulate alpha-receptors, though the reflex sympathetic discharge does release norepinephrine.
Incorrect. Reducing large artery stiffness would decrease afterload, not increase it.
Incorrect. Rapid-acting vasodilators cause reflex *tachycardia* (increased rate), which *shortens* diastole and potentially worsens ischemia.
Incorrect. Vasodilators generally decrease preload (filling pressure), though arteriolar-selective ones like nifedipine have less effect on preload than nitrates.
citation: In book "Mini Katzung", Page 109 (Book Page): The drop in blood pressure evokes increased sympathetic outflow to the cardiovascular system and increases heart rate and force of contraction... These changes can markedly increase cardiac oxygen requirement.

category: Define Coronary Steal Phenomenon
statement: A 68-year-old male with severe coronary atherosclerosis and stable angina of effort is prescribed prompt-release nifedipine for hypertension. Shortly after his first dose, he experiences an acute, crushing substernal chest pain. His vitals show a heart rate of 115 bpm and a blood pressure of 105/65 mmHg. What is the most likely pharmacological explanation for this adverse event?
options: Direct inhibition of the sinoatrial node leading to severe bradycardia.
Development of 'Monday disease' due to rapid tolerance of the vasodilator.
Reflex sympathetic outflow increasing O2 demand while coronary flow fails to match the requirement.
Activation of the VMAT pump leading to excessive catecholamine depletion.
Methemoglobinemia induced by the chemical structure of nifedipine.
correctOption: Reflex sympathetic outflow increasing O2 demand while coronary flow fails to match the requirement.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Nifedipine (a dihydropyridine) has minimal direct effects on the SA node compared to verapamil or diltiazem; its main effect is peripheral vasodilation.
Incorrect. 'Monday disease' is related to industrial exposure to organic nitrates and the cycle of tolerance/loss of tolerance, not acute nifedipine dosing.

Correct. The prompt-release formulation caused a rapid BP drop, leading to reflex tachycardia (115 bpm). This increased the myocardial oxygen demand (double product) beyond what the obstructed coronary flow could provide, triggering ischemia.
Incorrect. VMAT (vesicle monoamine transporter) inhibition is the mechanism of reserpine, not nifedipine.
Incorrect. Methemoglobinemia is a toxicity associated with nitrites (e.g., amyl nitrite), not calcium channel blockers like nifedipine.
citation: In book "Mini Katzung", Page 109 (Book Page): Rapid-acting vasodilators—such as nifedipine in its prompt-release formulation—cause significant and sudden reduction in blood pressure. The drop in blood pressure evokes increased sympathetic outflow... If coronary blood flow does not increase sufficiently to match the increased requirement, ischemia and infarction can result.

category: Define Coronary Steal Phenomenon
statement: During the induction of 'coronary steal,' a potent vasodilator acts on the resistance vessels of the heart. Which specific pharmacodynamic step differentiates the response of ischemic tissue from healthy tissue in this scenario?
options: Ischemic tissue vessels are already maximally dilated by local metabolites, losing their ability to dilate further.
Ischemic tissue lacks the ALDH2 enzyme required to process arteriolar vasodilators.
Healthy tissue vessels constrict in response to local ischemia in distant zones.
The double product in ischemic tissue is reduced due to a localized increase in ejection time.
Potent vasodilators specifically target the fixed atheromatous plaques, causing them to constrict.
correctOption: Ischemic tissue vessels are already maximally dilated by local metabolites, losing their ability to dilate further.
optionExplanations: Correct. In atherosclerotic angina, vessels distal to an obstruction are often already dilated by local metabolites (like lactic acid) to maintain flow. Global vasodilators dilate healthy vessels, which reduces the pressure gradient and 'steals' blood away from the already-dilated ischemic vessels.
Incorrect. While ALDH2 is needed for nitrates, it is not the general reason for the failure of global arteriolar vasodilators in steal.
Incorrect. Healthy vessels dilate in response to the drug, which is the exact cause of the diversion of flow away from the ischemic zone (Coronary Steal).
Incorrect. The double product is a measure of total cardiac work (HR x Systolic BP) and is not localized to one tissue zone.
Incorrect. Fixed atheromatous plaques are physical obstructions and do not constrict or dilate; the vessels *around* or *distal* to them do.
citation: In book "Mini Katzung", Page 103 (Book Page): When cardiac work increases (eg, in exercise), the obstruction of flow and inadequate oxygen delivery results in the accumulation of metabolites, eg, lactic acid, and ischemic changes that stimulate myocardial pain endings.

category: Define Coronary Steal Phenomenon
statement: Which of the following classes of drugs is most frequently associated with the risk of precipitating myocardial ischemia due to rapid blood pressure reduction and reflex cardiac stimulation, contributing to the 'ineffective' profile of coronary vasodilators?
options: Selective Beta-1 blockers
Prompt-release Dihydropyridine Calcium Channel Blockers
Long-acting Organic Nitrates
Angiotensin Converting Enzyme (ACE) Inhibitors
Potassium-sparing Diuretics
correctOption: Prompt-release Dihydropyridine Calcium Channel Blockers
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Beta-blockers reduce heart rate and cardiac work, actually protecting against the tachycardia that contributes to ischemia.
Correct. Prompt-release DHPs (like nifedipine) cause rapid vasodilation and reflex sympathetic discharge, which are the primary drivers of the 'ineffective' and potentially harmful effects in angina.
Incorrect. Long-acting nitrates are standard prophylaxis for angina and do not typically cause the sudden, sharp BP drops associated with prompt-release DHPs.
Incorrect. ACE inhibitors produce minimal compensatory responses and are generally well-tolerated in heart failure and hypertension without triggering significant reflex tachycardia.
Incorrect. Diuretics reduce blood volume and do not cause the rapid arteriolar dilation associated with the coronary steal or reflex tachycardia phenomenon.
citation: In book "Mini Katzung", Page 109 (Book Page): Several studies have suggested that patients receiving prompt-release nifedipine may have an increased risk of myocardial infarction. Slow-release formulations do not seem to impose this risk.

category: Define Coronary Steal Phenomenon
statement: In the context of coronary steal, what happens to the 'Double Product' when a patient is given a potent, rapid-acting arteriolar vasodilator?
options: It decreases significantly due to the reduction in both heart rate and systolic BP.
It only increases if the patient is also taking a beta-blocker.
It becomes an unreliable measure of cardiac work in the presence of calcium channel blockers.
It may increase due to a marked reflex increase in heart rate despite the decrease in systolic BP.
It remains constant because the decrease in BP is exactly offset by a decrease in heart rate.
correctOption: It may increase due to a marked reflex increase in heart rate despite the decrease in systolic BP.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. While BP decreases, heart rate *increases* via reflex, so a significant decrease in the product is not guaranteed and often moves in the opposite direction.
Incorrect. Beta-blockers *prevent* the reflex tachycardia, meaning the double product would more likely *decrease* if the patient were taking one.
Incorrect. The double product remains a valid clinical estimate of cardiac work and oxygen requirement regardless of the drug class used.

Correct. Because the double product is Heart Rate x Systolic BP, a dramatic reflex increase in heart rate (sympathetic tone) can cause the total product to rise, increasing oxygen demand even as BP falls.
Incorrect. The reflex tachycardia is often substantial, and the balance is not usually equal, often leading to a net increase in oxygen demand.
citation: In book "Mini Katzung", Page 105 (Book Page): Heart rate and systolic blood pressure may be multiplied to yield the double product, a measure of cardiac work... the double product is sensitive to sympathetic tone.

category: Define Coronary Steal Phenomenon
statement: A 55-year-old patient with chronic stable angina and a history of myocardial infarction is being managed for hypertension. The physician avoids using potent arteriolar vasodilators like hydralazine as monotherapy. What is the most critical pharmacological reason to avoid such agents in this patient's anginal management?
options: They increase venous tone, leading to increased preload.
They directly inhibit the formation of nitric oxide in the endothelium.
They cause reflex tachycardia and increased force of contraction, worsening the oxygen supply-demand mismatch.
They induce a lupus-like syndrome that specifically targets the coronary arteries.
They have a very long duration of action that makes them unsuitable for acute attacks.
correctOption: They cause reflex tachycardia and increased force of contraction, worsening the oxygen supply-demand mismatch.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Arteriolar vasodilators like hydralazine *reduce* tone, not increase it, and they have little effect on the venous system.
Incorrect. Hydralazine actually *increases* the release of nitric oxide from endothelial cells; it does not inhibit it.

Correct. Potent vasodilators like hydralazine trigger the baroreceptor reflex, leading to increased sympathetic outflow. This increases heart rate and contractility, which are detrimental to a patient with limited coronary reserve.
Incorrect. While hydralazine can cause a lupus-like syndrome (Page 104), it is not the *critical* pharmacological reason for its failure in managing acute angina symptoms; the reflex tachycardia is.
Incorrect. Hydralazine has a duration of hours (not minutes), but its 'ineffectiveness' in angina is due to its physiological reflex effects, not its duration.
citation: In book "Mini Katzung", Page 107 (Book Page): Significant reflex tachycardia and increased force of contraction are common results when nitroglycerin reduces the blood pressure... These compensatory effects result from the baroreceptor mechanism.

category: Define Coronary Steal Phenomenon
statement: When comparing the effects of antianginal drugs, which variable is uniquely 'detrimental' as it increases myocardial oxygen requirement, and is often exacerbated by rapid-acting vasodilators?
options: Decreased heart size
Decreased diastolic filling pressure
Decreased peripheral resistance
Shortened ejection time
Increased heart rate
correctOption: Increased heart rate
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Decreased heart size (reduced preload) is a beneficial effect as it reduces fiber tension and oxygen demand.
Incorrect. Decreased diastolic filling pressure (preload) is beneficial for reducing oxygen requirement.
Incorrect. Decreased peripheral resistance (reduced afterload) is generally beneficial as it reduces the work the heart must do to eject blood.

Incorrect. Shortened ejection time (when occurring with a reflex increase in heart rate) is associated with increased sympathetic tone, but the *primary* detrimental driver in the context of vasodilators is the rate itself.

Correct. An increased heart rate is detrimental because it increases oxygen requirement and shortens the time available for coronary perfusion (diastole). This is the hallmark of the reflex response to rapid-acting vasodilators.
citation: In book "Mini Katzung", Page 108 (Book Page): Actions include both beneficial antianginal effects (decreased heart rate, cardiac force, blood pressure) and detrimental effects (increased heart size, longer ejection period; Table 12–1).

category: Define Coronary Steal Phenomenon
statement: Which of the following is an anatomical determinant of myocardial oxygen requirement that global vasodilators might paradoxically increase through reflex mechanisms, thus worsening ischemia?
options: Gastrointestinal motility
Intramyocardial fiber tension
Renal renin secretion
Mitochondrial aldehyde dehydrogenase activity
Nitric oxide concentration
correctOption: Intramyocardial fiber tension
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Gastrointestinal motility has no direct relationship to myocardial oxygen requirement.

Correct. Fiber tension is the primary determinant of oxygen demand. Reflex increases in contractility and heart size (if preload is not managed) increase this tension, worsening ischemia in the 'steal' or 'reflex' context.
Incorrect. While renin secretion increases as a compensatory response to vasodilators, it is a hormonal/biochemical response, not the direct anatomic determinant of myocardial O2 demand.
Incorrect. ALDH2 is an enzyme involved in nitrate metabolism, not a determinant of oxygen requirement.
Incorrect. Nitric oxide is a signaling molecule, not an anatomical determinant of oxygen requirement.
citation: In book "Mini Katzung", Page 104 (Book Page): A major determinant is myocardial fiber tension (the higher the tension, the greater the oxygen requirement).

category: Define Coronary Steal Phenomenon
coreConcept: Inaccuracy of the term Coronary Vasodilator
statement: What is the primary hemodynamic reason that 'coronary vasodilator' is considered an older, incorrect name for effective antianginal drugs?
options: Potent vasodilators may fail to increase delivery to ischemic zones and can actually prove ineffective or harmful in angina.
Vasodilators are only effective in treating the vasospastic form of Prinzmetal's angina, not classic effort angina.
Most coronary vasodilators have a very high first-pass effect, making them biologically unavailable via the oral route.
These drugs primarily work by increasing the double product, which is detrimental in atherosclerotic angina.
They act solely on venous tone, which does not impact the myocardial oxygen requirement or delivery.
correctOption: Potent vasodilators may fail to increase delivery to ischemic zones and can actually prove ineffective or harmful in angina.
optionExplanations: The term is considered incorrect because simple vasodilation does not guarantee relief. In many cases, potent vasodilators can divert blood away from ischemic areas (the steal phenomenon) or fail to provide a net increase in flow to the areas that need it most, making them clinically ineffective.

While vasodilators like nitrates and calcium channel blockers are indeed effective for vasospastic angina, they are also the cornerstone for treating classic atherosclerotic (effort) angina by reducing oxygen demand.

While some drugs like nitroglycerin have high first-pass metabolism, this is a pharmacokinetic property of specific agents, not a reason why the classification 'coronary vasodilator' is conceptually incorrect for the entire class of antianginal therapy.

The double product is a measure of cardiac work (heart rate x systolic blood pressure); effective antianginal drugs typically reduce the double product to decrease oxygen requirement, rather than increasing it.
Vasodilators act on both veins (reducing preload) and arteries (reducing afterload), both of which are critical determinants of the myocardial oxygen requirement.
citation: In book "Mini Katzung", Page 104 (Book Page): Coronary vasodilator Older, incorrect name for drugs useful in angina; some potent coronary vasodilators are ineffective in angina

category: Define Coronary Steal Phenomenon
statement: Which of the following pathophysiological mechanisms best explains how a potent vasodilator can exacerbate myocardial ischemia in a patient with a fixed atherosclerotic plaque?
options: The drug stimulates endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS) in normal vessels but inhibits it in ischemic vessels.
Inhibition of the Na+/K+/2Cl- transporter in the thick ascending limb leads to hypercalcemia and coronary spasm.
Dilating the epicardial vessels leads to a sudden increase in the late sodium current within the myocytes.
Activation of mitochondrial aldehyde dehydrogenase-2 (ALDH2) causes the selective constriction of collateral vessels.
Vasodilation in non-ischemic regions reduces the pressure gradient available to drive blood flow through collateral vessels to ischemic zones.
correctOption: Vasodilation in non-ischemic regions reduces the pressure gradient available to drive blood flow through collateral vessels to ischemic zones.
optionExplanations: Vasodilators do not typically have opposing effects on eNOS based on the ischemia status of the vessel; the mechanism of 'steal' is hemodynamic, not biochemical inhibition of eNOS.
This describes the mechanism of loop diuretics, not coronary vasodilators or the steal phenomenon.
The late sodium current is an electrical phenomenon targeted by drugs like ranolazine; it is not the primary mechanism of vasodilator-induced ischemia.
ALDH2 is the enzyme that bioactivates nitrates to release NO; it is involved in relaxation, not the selective constriction of collateral vessels.

This describes the 'steal' phenomenon. Arterioles in ischemic zones are already maximally dilated due to local metabolites. When a drug dilates arterioles in healthy, non-ischemic zones, it lowers the overall resistance in those areas, diverting flow away from the high-resistance, collateral-dependent ischemic areas.
citation: In book "Mini Katzung", Page 109 (Book Page): If coronary blood flow does not increase sufficiently to match the increased requirement, ischemia and infarction can result.

category: Define Coronary Steal Phenomenon
coreConcept: Demand vs. Delivery Strategy in Angina
statement: When comparing the clinical outcomes of antianginal therapy, what distinguishes 'effective' drugs like Nitrates from 'ineffective' pure coronary vasodilators?
options: Nitrates only increase oxygen delivery, whereas pure vasodilators only reduce oxygen requirement.
Nitrates act exclusively on the sinoatrial pacemaker current (If), preventing the reflex tachycardia seen with pure vasodilators.
Pure vasodilators increase the double product by reducing ejection time and increasing systolic fiber tension.
Effective drugs increase large artery stiffness to maintain the pressure gradient across the coronary bed.
Effective drugs prioritize reducing oxygen requirement over simply increasing coronary flow via general vasodilation.
correctOption: Effective drugs prioritize reducing oxygen requirement over simply increasing coronary flow via general vasodilation.
optionExplanations: The opposite is often true; nitrates are highly effective at reducing oxygen requirement by decreasing preload (venodilation) and afterload.
Nitrates do not act on the If current; that is the mechanism for ivabradine. Nitrates often cause reflex tachycardia due to baroreceptor activation.

Pure vasodilators typically decrease blood pressure, which should theoretically decrease the double product, but they may cause a reflex increase in heart rate that offsets this, potentially increasing the double product.
Effective antianginal drugs do not increase arterial stiffness; stiffness is a determinant of afterload that increases the heart's oxygen requirement, which is undesirable in angina therapy.

Effective antianginal therapy focuses on the balance between requirement and delivery. Drugs that just dilate coronaries (pure vasodilators) might not help because the ischemic area's vessels are already dilated, and a drop in systemic pressure might actually reduce the perfusion of that area.
citation: In book "Mini Katzung", Page 104 (Book Page): Coronary vasodilator: Older, incorrect name for drugs useful in angina; some potent coronary vasodilators are ineffective in angina.

category: Define Coronary Steal Phenomenon
statement: A 64-year-old male with a history of stable angina of effort is prescribed a prompt-release formulation of a potent dihydropyridine vasodilator. Shortly after taking the first dose, he experiences a severe, prolonged anginal attack. Which hemodynamic sequence most likely precipitated this adverse event?
options: Sudden reduction in blood pressure evoking reflex sympathetic outflow that increases heart rate and force.
Preferential dilation of veins over arterioles, leading to a critical drop in cardiac output and systemic perfusion.
Marked increase in venous tone leading to excessive diastolic filling and fiber tension.
Inhibition of the mitochondrial aldehyde dehydrogenase-2 enzyme leading to a toxic accumulation of acetaldehyde.
Selective blockade of N-type calcium channels in the heart, leading to paradoxical sympathetic stimulation.
correctOption: Sudden reduction in blood pressure evoking reflex sympathetic outflow that increases heart rate and force.
optionExplanations: Prompt-release formulations cause rapid vasodilation and a sharp drop in blood pressure. This triggers the baroreceptor reflex, resulting in sympathetic discharge that increases heart rate and contractility, sharply raising the heart's oxygen demand beyond what the compromised coronaries can deliver.
Dihydropyridines are relatively selective for arterioles over veins; the issue is the reflex increase in demand, not a selective venous effect.
Vasodilators decrease venous tone, not increase it. Increased venous tone would increase preload, which is not the typical effect of these agents.
ALDH2 is involved in nitrate metabolism, but its 'inhibition' is not the cause of ischemia; rather, its action is required for the efficacy of nitrates.

Calcium channel blockers used in angina target L-type channels, not N-type channels (which are found in nerve endings). Their effect on L-type channels in the heart (verapamil/diltiazem) is usually cardiodepressant, not stimulatory.
citation: In book "Mini Katzung", Page 109 (Book Page): Rapid-acting vasodilators—such as nifedipine in its prompt-release formulation—cause significant and sudden reduction in blood pressure. The drop in blood pressure evokes increased sympathetic outflow to the cardiovascular system and increases heart rate and force of contraction... These changes can markedly increase cardiac oxygen requirement.

category: Define Coronary Steal Phenomenon
statement: In the context of the 'Coronary Steal' phenomenon, why might a drug that increases coronary collateral flow be superior to a pure arterial vasodilator?
options: Increasing collateral flow specifically reduces the double product by inhibiting systolic fiber tension.
Collateral flow ensures that oxygen delivery is increased specifically to the ischemic myocardium regardless of systemic resistance.
Pure arterial vasodilators always induce methemoglobinemia, which reduces the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood.
Collateral vessels are less sensitive to the baroreceptor reflex than the main coronary arteries.
Only pure arterial vasodilators act by increasing intracellular cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP).
correctOption: Collateral flow ensures that oxygen delivery is increased specifically to the ischemic myocardium regardless of systemic resistance.
optionExplanations: Collateral flow increases delivery; it does not directly reduce the double product. The double product is reduced by lowering heart rate and blood pressure (reducing demand).

Nitrates are beneficial partly because they can increase flow through collateral vessels directly into ischemic areas, whereas pure vasodilators might just dilate healthy vessels and 'steal' blood away from those collaterals.
Only nitrites (not nitrates or general vasodilators) cause methemoglobinemia at high concentrations.
Collateral vessels are not 'insensitive' to reflexes, but the benefit of collateral flow is about the anatomical distribution of blood to ischemic zones, not a unique reflex property.
Nitrates (which are effective) act by increasing cGMP; many vasodilators act via other mechanisms like potassium channel opening or calcium channel blockade.
citation: In book "Mini Katzung", Page 107 (Book Page): A secondary mechanism—namely, an increase in coronary flow via collateral vessels in ischemic areas—may also contribute.

category: Define Coronary Steal Phenomenon
statement: Which of the following is a recognized clinical indicator of a 'Coronary Steal' effect occurring during the administration of a rapid-acting vasodilator?
options: Development of a lupus-like syndrome that is reversible upon drug discontinuation.
A significant increase in serum uric acid levels leading to an acute gouty attack.
Increased PR interval on the electrocardiogram.
Ischemia or infarction resulting from an imbalance where coronary flow fails to match an increased requirement.
Sudden onset of hirsutism due to the opening of potassium channels in the skin.
correctOption: Ischemia or infarction resulting from an imbalance where coronary flow fails to match an increased requirement.
optionExplanations: Lupus-like syndrome is a specific toxicity associated with hydralazine or procainamide, unrelated to the acute hemodynamic steal phenomenon.
Increased uric acid (hyperuricemia) is a side effect of thiazide and loop diuretics, not vasodilators or the steal phenomenon.
Increased PR interval is a sign of AV nodal delay, typically seen with verapamil, diltiazem, or beta-blockers, not a marker of coronary steal.

The hallmark of an ineffective or 'stealing' vasodilator is that it may drop perfusion pressure or trigger reflex demand such that the myocardium becomes more ischemic, potentially leading to infarction.
Hirsutism is a side effect of minoxidil, a potassium channel opener, but it is a chronic skin effect, not a diagnostic indicator of acute coronary steal.
citation: In book "Mini Katzung", Page 109 (Book Page): If coronary blood flow does not increase sufficiently to match the increased requirement, ischemia and infarction can result.

category: Define Coronary Steal Phenomenon
statement: A patient with effort angina is given a drug that successfully reduces myocardial oxygen requirement by decreasing preload. How does this strategy compare to the risk of coronary steal associated with pure coronary vasodilators?
options: It is more dangerous because reducing preload always leads to a reflex increase in afterload.
Decreasing preload specifically prevents the synthesis of cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP), avoiding hypotension.
This strategy is identical to the mechanism of pure vasodilators, meaning the risk of steal is unchanged.
It is safer because it decreases the intramyocardial fiber tension, which is a primary determinant of oxygen demand.
Reducing preload is only effective if the drug also blocks L-type calcium channels in the skeletal muscle.
correctOption: It is safer because it decreases the intramyocardial fiber tension, which is a primary determinant of oxygen demand.
optionExplanations: Reducing preload (venodilation) does not 'always' lead to a reflex increase in afterload; in fact, many antianginal drugs (like nitrates) reduce both, though the venous effect usually predominates.
Nitrates *increase* cGMP to cause relaxation; they do not prevent its synthesis. Blocking cGMP synthesis would cause vasoconstriction, not vasodilation.
The strategies are different; reducing demand (via preload/afterload) is the proven therapeutic goal, whereas 'pure' coronary vasodilation is often an ineffective 'older' approach.

Nitrates reduce preload (venous return), which reduces the heart's size and fiber tension (oxygen demand). This 'demand-side' strategy is generally safer and more effective in stable angina than attempting to 'force' more flow via non-selective vasodilation.
Calcium channel blockers do not significantly affect skeletal muscle because skeletal muscle relies on intracellular calcium stores, not extracellular influx through L-type channels.
citation: In book "Mini Katzung", Page 105 (Book Page): A major determinant is myocardial fiber tension (the higher the tension, the greater the oxygen requirement).

category: Define Coronary Steal Phenomenon
statement: A 70-year-old patient with a fixed 90% stenosis in the Right Coronary Artery (RCA) is participating in a clinical trial. Drug X is a 'potent coronary vasodilator' that has no effect on heart rate or venous tone. Drug Y is a Beta-blocker. Why is Drug X likely to perform poorly in this patient compared to Drug Y?
options: Drug X will cause a reflex tachycardia that Drug Y prevents by blocking If currents.
Drug X increases the risk of 'Monday Disease' by causing rapid tolerance over the weekend.
Drug X may divert blood to vessels with lower resistance in healthy areas, while Drug Y reduces the overall demand of the RCA-supplied muscle.
Drug X will decrease diastolic filling time, while Drug Y will increase it by slowing the heart rate.
Drug Y increases the double product, which improves the oxygen delivery-to-demand ratio.
correctOption: Drug X may divert blood to vessels with lower resistance in healthy areas, while Drug Y reduces the overall demand of the RCA-supplied muscle.
optionExplanations: Drug X is stated to have 'no effect on heart rate', so reflex tachycardia isn't the issue here. Also, beta-blockers block beta-receptors, not If currents (that's ivabradine).
Monday Disease is a phenomenon of nitrate tolerance in industrial workers (explosives factories), not a general property of 'pure' vasodilators like Drug X.

This is the classic 'Coronary Steal'. Drug X dilates all coronary arterioles. The ones in the 90% stenosis zone are already dilated by local metabolites. Dilation in healthy zones lowers resistance there, 'stealing' flow from the stenotic zone. Drug Y avoids this by lowering the muscle's metabolic demand.
If Drug X has no effect on heart rate, it won't change diastolic filling time. Drug Y (Beta-blocker) does increase diastole, but the main 'steal' issue with X is blood diversion.
Beta-blockers *decrease* the double product (Heart Rate x Blood Pressure), which is beneficial because it signifies reduced cardiac work and oxygen demand.
citation: In book "Mini Katzung", Page 104 (Book Page): some potent coronary vasodilators are ineffective in angina. ... Page 109 (Book Page): Slow-release formulations do not seem to impose this risk.

category: Define Coronary Steal Phenomenon
statement: In the physiological regulation of coronary flow, why is a sudden reduction in systemic blood pressure from a vasodilator particularly dangerous in the presence of atherosclerotic obstructions?
options: Low blood pressure stimulates the V1 receptors in the heart, causing a paradoxical increase in venous return.
It causes the opening of potassium channels, which leads to the hyperpolarization of the sinoatrial node and cardiac arrest.
The reduction in pressure prevents the mitochondrial aldehyde dehydrogenase-2 from releasing nitric oxide.
It reduces the perfusion pressure across the obstruction while simultaneously increasing demand via reflex tachycardia.
It triggers the release of renin, which directly constricts the coronary collateral vessels.
correctOption: It reduces the perfusion pressure across the obstruction while simultaneously increasing demand via reflex tachycardia.
optionExplanations: V1 receptors are for Vasopressin and cause vasoconstriction; they do not increase venous return in response to low blood pressure in a way that helps angina.
While potassium channel openers (like minoxidil) cause hyperpolarization in smooth muscle, they don't typically cause cardiac arrest via SA node hyperpolarization in clinical antianginal doses.
ALDH2 activity is dependent on the presence of the drug (nitrates) and local cellular conditions, not directly on the systemic blood pressure level.

This is a dual-threat mechanism: (1) Lower systemic pressure reduces the 'push' of blood through narrowed arteries, and (2) the body's reflex response to that low pressure increases heart work (demand). This mismatch is what defines the failure of certain vasodilators.
Renin release leads to Angiotensin II production, which is a systemic vasoconstrictor, but the primary acute problem in 'steal' is the reflex sympathetic (catecholamine) surge.
citation: In book "Mini Katzung", Page 109 (Book Page): Rapid-acting vasodilators... cause significant and sudden reduction in blood pressure. The drop in blood pressure evokes increased sympathetic outflow... increases heart rate and force... If coronary blood flow does not increase sufficiently to match the increased requirement, ischemia and infarction can result.

category: Define Coronary Steal Phenomenon
statement: Which specific formulation of calcium channel blockers was historically associated with an increased risk of myocardial infarction because of its rapid vasodilator effects?
options: Slow-release verapamil
Transdermal diltiazem
Intravenous nicardipine infusion
Oral sustained-release amlodipine
Prompt-release nifedipine
correctOption: Prompt-release nifedipine
optionExplanations: Slow-release formulations (including verapamil) do not typically cause the sudden, sharp drop in blood pressure that triggers the dangerous reflex tachycardia associated with MI risk.
Diltiazem is not typically administered via a transdermal patch for angina; nitroglycerin is the prototype for transdermal delivery.

While intravenous nicardipine is a potent vasodilator, its use in controlled hospital settings (infusion) allows for careful titration, unlike the 'bolus' effect of taking a prompt-release oral tablet.
Amlodipine is naturally long-acting (long half-life) and does not typically evoke the same level of acute reflex tachycardia seen with prompt-release nifedipine.

Prompt-release (rapid-acting) nifedipine was found to cause sudden hypotension and a compensatory sympathetic surge that increased myocardial oxygen demand, leading to ischemia and infarction in susceptible patients.
citation: In book "Mini Katzung", Page 109 (Book Page): several studies during the 1990s suggested that use of nifedipine was associated with an increased risk of myocardial infarction... Prompt-release nifedipine... cause significant and sudden reduction in blood pressure.

category: Define Coronary Steal Phenomenon
statement: A 62-year-old male with chronic effort angina and a 90% occlusion of the Left Anterior Descending (LAD) artery is administered a potent, rapid-acting arteriolar vasodilator. Instead of relief, he develops worsening chest pain. This 'coronary steal' phenomenon is best explained by which mechanism?
options: Preferential venodilation leading to a sudden increase in end-diastolic fiber tension.
A direct negative inotropic effect reducing the pressure gradient across the fixed obstruction.
Inhibition of the Na+/K+ ATPase pump in the ischemic myocardium causing calcium overload.
Dilation of resistance vessels in non-ischemic zones diverting blood away from maximally dilated ischemic areas.
Dilation of epicardial collateral vessels leading to increased flow to the ischemic zone.
correctOption: Dilation of resistance vessels in non-ischemic zones diverting blood away from maximally dilated ischemic areas.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Venodilation (the primary effect of nitrates) reduces preload and end-diastolic fiber tension, which is the opposite of this description and is beneficial in angina.
Incorrect. A negative inotropic effect (seen with verapamil/diltiazem) would reduce oxygen demand, which generally treats angina rather than causing a 'steal' effect.

Incorrect. Inhibition of Na+/K+ ATPase is the mechanism of cardiac glycosides (digoxin), not the mechanism of vasodilators associated with coronary steal or angina therapy complications described in the text (Chapter 12).

Correct. Coronary steal occurs when a potent vasodilator dilates resistance vessels (arterioles) in well-perfused (non-ischemic) areas. Because vessels in the ischemic zone are already maximally dilated by local metabolites, the drug-induced dilation in healthy zones lowers the pressure and 'steals' blood flow away from the ischemic zone.
Incorrect. Dilation of epicardial collateral vessels is a beneficial secondary mechanism associated with nitrates, which helps increase delivery to ischemic areas rather than stealing from them.
citation: In book "Mini Katzung", Page 104 (Book Page): [Coronary vasodilator] Older, incorrect name for drugs useful in angina; some potent coronary vasodilators are ineffective in angina

category: Define Coronary Steal Phenomenon
coreConcept: Inadequacy of Global Vasodilation in Fixed Obstruction
statement: In the pathophysiology of coronary steal, why are 'potent coronary vasodilators' often described as 'ineffective' in the management of atherosclerotic angina?
options: They exclusively dilate epicardial vessels which have no impact on myocardial perfusion.
They increase large artery stiffness, thereby increasing afterload and oxygen demand.
These agents primarily act on the venous system, which does not affect the double product.
They inhibit aldehyde dehydrogenase-2 (ALDH2), preventing the release of nitric oxide.
The ischemic tissue already possesses maximally dilated resistance vessels due to metabolite accumulation.
correctOption: The ischemic tissue already possesses maximally dilated resistance vessels due to metabolite accumulation.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Potent vasodilators that cause steal usually act on resistance vessels (arterioles). Dilation of epicardial vessels is actually a goal of effective therapy like nitrates to bypass obstructions.

Incorrect. Vasodilators reduce vascular resistance (afterload), they do not increase stiffness. The 'ineffectiveness' mentioned in the text refers to the lack of oxygen delivery to the specifically ischemic zones.
Incorrect. Venous dilation *does* affect the double product by reducing preload and cardiac work. Steal is associated with arteriolar, not venous, dominance.

Incorrect. Inhibiting ALDH2 would prevent the action of nitrates (Page 113), but 'potent coronary vasodilators' associated with steal act through mechanisms that bypass this or act directly on arterioles (e.g., potassium channel openers).

Correct. In atherosclerotic angina, the vessels downstream of a fixed obstruction are already maximally dilated by local ischemic metabolites (like lactic acid) to maintain flow. Global vasodilators only affect healthy vessels, creating a pressure gradient that favors flow to non-ischemic regions.
citation: In book "Mini Katzung", Page 104 (Book Page): [Atherosclerotic angina] is associated with atheromatous plaques that partially occlude one or more coronary arteries... resulting in the accumulation of metabolites, eg, lactic acid... [Coronary vasodilator] Older, incorrect name for drugs useful in angina; some potent coronary vasodilators are ineffective in angina

category: Define Coronary Steal Phenomenon
statement: A researcher is comparing the effects of Nitroglycerin and a potent arteriolar vasodilator on myocardial perfusion. Unlike the 'steal' effect seen with the latter, Nitroglycerin is effective in angina because it:
options: Increases afterload to maintain a higher perfusion pressure across the plaque.
Acts exclusively by increasing the heart rate to improve the double product.
Primarily relaxes epicardial vessels and improves flow through collaterals.
Prevents the formation of lactic acid by shifting metabolism to fatty acids.
Selectively dilates resistance arterioles only in the ischemic subendocardium.
correctOption: Primarily relaxes epicardial vessels and improves flow through collaterals.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Nitrates *reduce* afterload via arteriolar dilation at higher doses; they do not increase it. Increased afterload would worsen oxygen demand.
Incorrect. Increasing heart rate (tachycardia) is a compensatory reflex that is *detrimental* because it increases oxygen requirement and shortens diastole, the time for coronary flow.

Correct. The text notes that nitrates increase flow through partially occluded epicardial vessels and increase flow via collateral vessels. This improves delivery specifically to the ischemic area, unlike steal agents that divert it away.
Incorrect. Shifting metabolism from fatty acids to glucose is the mechanism of pFOX inhibitors like ranolazine (Page 112), not nitrates.
Incorrect. Nitrates do not selectively dilate ischemic arterioles; their primary therapeutic benefit is venodilation (preload reduction) and epicardial dilation.
citation: In book "Mini Katzung", Page 107 (Book Page): Relaxation of arterial smooth muscle may increase flow through partially occluded epicardial coronary vessels... A secondary mechanism—namely, an increase in coronary flow via collateral vessels in ischemic areas—may also contribute.

category: Define Coronary Steal Phenomenon
statement: A 68-year-old patient with a history of classic angina and fixed coronary stenosis is given a prompt-release formulation of nifedipine for hypertension. Within 30 minutes, the patient experiences severe angina and an ECG shows ST-segment depression. Which multi-step process described in the 'Skill Keeper' most likely caused this outcome?
options: Verapamil-like inhibition of the SA node leading to severe bradycardia and hypotension.
Sudden reduction in blood pressure triggering increased sympathetic outflow, which increases oxygen demand beyond delivery capacity.
Induction of a lupus-like syndrome resulting in acute pericardial inflammation.
Direct stimulation of the vasomotor center in the brainstem causing paradoxical vasoconstriction.
Potassium channel opening leading to hyperpolarization and reduced coronary perfusion pressure.
correctOption: Sudden reduction in blood pressure triggering increased sympathetic outflow, which increases oxygen demand beyond delivery capacity.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Nifedipine is a dihydropyridine; it has a weak cardiac effect and does *not* cause bradycardia; it typically causes reflex tachycardia. Verapamil/Diltiazem are the ones that slow the SA node (Page 115).

Correct. The 'Skill Keeper' explains that rapid-acting vasodilators like nifedipine cause reflex tachycardia and increased contractility via sympathetic outflow. This increases demand. In the presence of fixed obstruction, the heart cannot increase delivery to match this demand, causing ischemia.
Incorrect. Hydralazine, not nifedipine, is associated with a reversible lupus-like syndrome (Page 104).
Incorrect. Nifedipine acts directly on vascular smooth muscle L-type channels, not by stimulating the vasomotor center (which would actually decrease BP if it were an alpha-2 agonist like clonidine).
Incorrect. While potassium channel opening is a mechanism for some vasodilators (like minoxidil), nifedipine is an L-type calcium channel blocker.
citation: In book "Mini Katzung", Page 110 (Book Page): Rapid-acting vasodilators—such as nifedipine in its prompt-release formulation—cause significant and sudden reduction in blood pressure. The drop in blood pressure evokes increased sympathetic outflow to the cardiovascular system and increases heart rate and force of contraction... if coronary blood flow does not increase sufficiently to match the increased requirement, ischemia and infarction can result.

category: Define Coronary Steal Phenomenon
statement: Hydralazine is noted for causing significant baroreceptor homeostatic responses. If used alone in a patient with coronary artery disease, which interaction between demand and delivery could exacerbate myocardial ischemia?
options: Arteriolar dilation in non-ischemic zones paired with reflex-mediated increases in myocardial oxygen consumption.
Increased venous return leading to pulmonary congestion and reduced oxygen saturation.
Potassium channel blockade leading to a prolonged QT interval and torsades de pointes.
Decreased heart rate leading to excessive diastolic filling and ventricular wall tension.
Inactivation of nitric oxide resulting in widespread coronary vasospasm.
correctOption: Arteriolar dilation in non-ischemic zones paired with reflex-mediated increases in myocardial oxygen consumption.
optionExplanations: Correct. Hydralazine is an arteriolar dilator (older vasodilator) that does not dilate veins. In CAD, its arteriolar effect can cause steal (diverting flow), and its reflex effect (tachycardia/increased force) significantly raises oxygen demand, a dangerous combination for an ischemic heart.
Incorrect. Hydralazine has more effect on arterioles than veins (Page 104); it would reduce, not increase, venous return (preload) if it had venous effects, though they are minimal.
Incorrect. Hydralazine's mechanism involves Nitric Oxide, not potassium channel blockade (Minoxidil is the K+ opener, Page 104). It is not typically associated with QT prolongation.
Incorrect. Hydralazine causes tachycardia (increased heart rate) as a compensatory response, not a decrease (Page 102, Table 11-1).
Incorrect. Hydralazine *releases* or facilitates Nitric Oxide; it does not inactivate it.
citation: In book "Mini Katzung", Page 97 (Book Page): Hydralazine... acts through the release of nitric oxide... causes significant baroreceptor homeostatic responses and must be combined with other drugs, usually diuretics and β blockers.

category: Define Coronary Steal Phenomenon
statement: The text classifies certain antianginal terms as 'incorrect' or 'older' due to a failure to account for oxygen delivery dynamics. Which term is used to describe drugs that may inadvertently worsen ischemia via flow redistribution?
options: Sinoatrial pacemaker current inhibitor
Coronary vasodilator
Nitrate tolerance mediator
Negative inotropic agent
Partial fatty acid oxidation inhibitor
correctOption: Coronary vasodilator
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Sinoatrial pacemaker current (If) inhibitors like ivabradine are a newer strategy to reduce demand (Page 112).
Correct. The text explicitly lists 'Coronary vasodilator' as an older, incorrect name because some 'potent' vasodilators (which might cause steal) do not help or actually worsen angina.
Incorrect. Nitrate tolerance refers to the loss of effect with prolonged exposure (Page 111), not the redistribution of flow.
Incorrect. Negative inotropic agents (like beta-blockers) are effective and standard for angina prophylaxis.
Incorrect. pFOX inhibitors (ranolazine) are a newer strategy focusing on metabolic efficiency (Page 112).
citation: In book "Mini Katzung", Page 104 (Book Page): Coronary vasodilator - Older, incorrect name for drugs useful in angina; some potent coronary vasodilators are ineffective in angina

category: Define Coronary Steal Phenomenon
coreConcept: Double Product and Myocardial Oxygen Balance
statement: Which of the following describes the relationship between the 'Double Product' and the impact of a vasodilator that induces coronary steal?
options: The double product is a measure of venous tone and is unaffected by arteriolar steal.
The vasodilator reduces the double product, thereby increasing the ischemic threshold.
The vasodilator increases the double product via reflex tachycardia, while simultaneously failing to increase delivery to ischemic zones.
The double product remains constant because the decrease in systolic pressure is perfectly offset by the increase in heart rate.
The double product only increases if the patient is also taking a β blocker concurrently.
correctOption: The vasodilator increases the double product via reflex tachycardia, while simultaneously failing to increase delivery to ischemic zones.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. The double product is the product of heart rate and systolic BP, which are heavily influenced by arteriolar resistance and sympathetic tone, not just venous tone.
Incorrect. If it induces steal and reflex effects, it would *increase* the double product (via tachycardia) and *decrease* the threshold for ischemia.

Correct. A 'steal' agent (potent vasodilator) often triggers reflex tachycardia, raising the heart rate and the double product (oxygen demand). Simultaneously, it redistributes flow away from the ischemic zone, worsening the oxygen delivery/demand gap.
Incorrect. While they might move in opposite directions, they rarely offset perfectly; the reflex tachycardia is often 'marked' (as with minoxidil, Page 104) or 'significant' (nifedipine, Page 117).
Incorrect. A beta-blocker would *prevent* the increase in double product by blocking the reflex tachycardia (Page 115).
citation: In book "Mini Katzung", Page 105 (Book Page): Heart rate and systolic blood pressure may be multiplied to yield the double product, a measure of cardiac work and therefore of oxygen requirement... In patients with atherosclerotic angina, effective drugs reduce the double product.

category: Define Coronary Steal Phenomenon
coreConcept: Vascular Selectivity and Reflex Sympathetic Drive
statement: A patient with a known history of severe atherosclerotic coronary artery disease is treated with minoxidil for refractory hypertension. He is not currently on a beta-blocker. He suddenly presents with acute substernal crushing pain. Based on the mechanism of minoxidil, which two factors are likely contributing to this 'steal-like' ischemic event?
options: Marked salt/water retention and a reduction in the PR interval.
Alpha-1 receptor blockade and a decrease in hepatic blood flow.
Venodilation and a decrease in the double product.
Arteriolar-selective vasodilation and a marked baroreceptor-mediated increase in heart rate.
Decreased insulin release and hyperpolarization of atrial myocytes.
correctOption: Arteriolar-selective vasodilation and a marked baroreceptor-mediated increase in heart rate.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. While salt/water retention occurs, it does not typically cause acute angina as rapidly as the reflex tachycardia does.
Incorrect. Minoxidil is a direct vasodilator, not an alpha-1 blocker (like prazosin, Page 103).
Incorrect. Minoxidil does not cause significant venodilation, and it *increases* the double product via tachycardia.

Correct. Minoxidil is an extremely potent arteriolar-selective vasodilator (K+ channel opener). This selectivity promotes coronary steal (redistribution). Additionally, it causes 'marked' reflex tachycardia (baroreceptor response), which exponentially increases myocardial oxygen demand.
Incorrect. Decreased insulin release is associated with diazoxide, not minoxidil, in the context of insulinomas (Page 104).
citation: In book "Mini Katzung", Page 97 (Book Page): Minoxidil sulfate, is a potassium channel opener that hyperpolarizes and relaxes vascular smooth muscle. The compensatory responses to minoxidil (Figure 11–1) require the concomitant use of diuretics and β blockers. [Page 102 (Book Page), Table]: Marked tachycardia, salt and water retention.

category: Define Coronary Steal Phenomenon
coreConcept: Vascular Bed Sensitivity to Nitric Oxide
statement: Why does Nitroglycerin, despite being a vasodilator, avoid the typical coronary steal phenomenon seen with agents like Hydralazine or Minoxidil?
options: Nitroglycerin has a dominant effect on venous capacitance vessels, reducing preload rather than just arteriolar resistance.
Nitroglycerin inhibits the cGMP pathway in healthy coronary vessels while stimulating it in blocked ones.
Nitroglycerin is a prodrug that is only activated by ischemic cardiac tissue.
Nitroglycerin only works in the presence of hyperkalemia.
Nitroglycerin reduces the heart rate by acting as a partial agonist at beta-receptors.
correctOption: Nitroglycerin has a dominant effect on venous capacitance vessels, reducing preload rather than just arteriolar resistance.
optionExplanations: Correct. Steal is primarily an arteriolar phenomenon. Nitroglycerin's most sensitive targets are the veins (venodilation). By reducing preload (cardiac size and fiber tension), it decreases the oxygen *requirement* of the whole heart, which protects against the ischemia that might be induced by its milder arteriolar effects.
Incorrect. Nitroglycerin stimulates the cGMP pathway in all vascular smooth muscle where it is activated; it does not have this 'dual' inhibitory/stimulatory action.
Incorrect. Nitroglycerin is converted to NO in most smooth muscle cells via ALDH2, not just in ischemic tissue (Page 113).
Incorrect. Nitroglycerin's mechanism is independent of hyperkalemia; actually, its mechanism involves ALDH2 and NO-mediated cGMP increase.
Incorrect. Nitrates do not act on beta-receptors; they actually often cause *reflex* increases in heart rate (Page 114).
citation: In book "Mini Katzung", Page 106 (Book Page): Smooth muscle relaxation by nitrates leads to an important degree of venodilation, which results in reduced cardiac size and cardiac output through reduced preload. [Page 107 (Book Page)]: Some studies suggest that of the vascular beds, the veins are the most sensitive to nitric oxide, arteries less so, and arterioles least sensitive.

category: Define Coronary Steal Phenomenon
statement: In the 'High-Yield Terms to Learn' for Chapter 12, how is the term 'Coronary vasodilator' specifically critiqued in relation to clinical efficacy?
options: It is defined as a substance that only affects the pulmonary circulation.
It is described as a term for drugs that primarily act on the SA node.
It is restricted to describe only those drugs that open potassium channels.
It is defined as the only drug class capable of reversing myocardial infarction.
It is noted as an older, incorrect name because some such drugs are ineffective in angina.
correctOption: It is noted as an older, incorrect name because some such drugs are ineffective in angina.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. The term specifically refers to the coronary (heart) circulation.
Incorrect. Drugs acting on the SA node to reduce heart rate (like ivabradine) are 'rate inhibitors', not just 'coronary vasodilators'.
Incorrect. While some 'ineffective' vasodilators are potassium channel openers, the term is not restricted to them in the text.
Incorrect. No single drug class is 'the only' one capable of reversing MI; management is multifactorial and revascularization is preferred (Page 112).

Correct. The glossary identifies 'coronary vasodilator' as an older and incorrect term because just because a drug is a 'potent coronary vasodilator' (e.g., causes global dilation) does not mean it effectively treats angina (due to steal effects).
citation: In book "Mini Katzung", Page 104 (Book Page): Coronary vasodilator - Older, incorrect name for drugs useful in angina; some potent coronary vasodilators are ineffective in angina

category: Classify anti arrhythmic drugs
statement: Based on the Singh-Vaughan Williams classification system, which of the following agents is categorized as a Group 1B antiarrhythmic drug?
options: Amiodarone
Flecainide
Procainamide
Verapamil
Lidocaine
correctOption: Lidocaine
optionExplanations: Amiodarone is primarily classified as a Group 3 agent (potassium channel blocker), although it possesses properties of all four main Singh-Vaughan Williams classes.
Flecainide is the prototype Group 1C agent, distinguished by its powerful sodium channel blockade with negligible effects on the action potential duration or repolarization.
Procainamide is classified as a Group 1A agent, which is characterized by sodium channel blockade that also prolongs the action potential duration by blocking potassium channels.
Verapamil is the prototype Group 4 agent, which acts by blocking L-type calcium channels, specifically affecting the sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodes.

Lidocaine is the prototype Group 1B agent; these drugs are characterized by their ability to block sodium channels in the inactivated state, particularly in depolarized or ischemic tissue, and they tend to shorten or have no effect on action potential duration in normal tissue.
citation: In book "Mini Katzung", Page 124 (Book Page): Group 1B drugs (prototype lidocaine) shorten the AP in some cardiac tissues, especially Purkinje fibers.

category: Classify anti arrhythmic drugs
statement: In the classification of Group 1 antiarrhythmic agents, what physiological parameter primarily differentiates Group 1A, 1B, and 1C drugs?
options: The rate of dissociation from M2 muscarinic receptors
The effect on the action potential duration (APD)
The selectivity for L-type calcium channels
The blockade of beta-adrenoceptors in the SA node
The effect on the PR interval duration
correctOption: The effect on the action potential duration (APD)
optionExplanations: While some Group 1A drugs (like quinidine) have antimuscarinic effects, this is not the primary physiological criterion for the sub-classification of the Group 1 sodium channel blockers.

Group 1 agents are subdivided based on their effect on the action potential duration: Group 1A prolongs the APD, Group 1B shortens it (especially in Purkinje fibers), and Group 1C has no significant effect on APD.
L-type calcium channel blockade is the defining characteristic of Group 4 agents, not the differentiation within Group 1 sodium channel blockers.
